# On the Small Rebellions of Daily Life

There's something quietly revolutionary about the mundane. Not in the way revolutionary is typically understood—not fireworks and proclamations and history books—but in the gentle, persistent way that ordinary people reshape their existence through small, deliberate choices.

I've been thinking about this while observing how people make coffee. There's a woman I imagine (I don't know her, but I imagine her anyway) who takes exactly seven minutes to make her morning coffee. Not six, not eight. Seven. She's chosen a particular grind, a particular water temperature, a particular ritual that she repeats with the consistency of a monk at prayer. In a world that constantly demands she optimize, accelerate, and monetize her time, this seven-minute ceremony is an act of resistance. It says: I will not be rushed. My morning belongs to me.

This is what I mean about small rebellions.

We live in an age of unprecedented connectivity and constraint. There are more ways to stay in touch than ever before, yet more sophisticated ways to surveil and monetize human attention. There are more conveniences available to us than any previous generation could imagine, yet somehow we feel more pressed for time. It's paradoxical, and I think it's because convenience was sold to us as freedom when what it actually delivers is dependency. Every convenience ties us to some system, some algorithm, some invisible machinery.

So people find ways to rebel. Not through dramatic gesture, but through the assertion of sovereignty in small domains. Someone decides to read physical books instead of scrolling on screens. Someone else chooses to take the long route home, walking instead of driving. A person decides to remember phone numbers instead of relying entirely on their device. These choices often make life incrementally harder, which is precisely the point.

The hardness is the freedom.

I think this is why gardening has become so popular, especially after 2020. People discovered that growing even a small plant on a windowsill creates a site of genuine autonomy. You cannot gamify a tomato plant. You cannot optimize its growth through a subscription service. You can only tend it, show up for it, fail with it, and occasionally succeed. There's no algorithm standing between you and the biological reality of whether it lives or dies. In that relationship, you are not a user or a consumer or an optimization target. You are simply a person caring for a living thing.

I'm drawn to these small acts of reclamation because I think they're how we remain human in an increasingly inhuman world. Not through grand refusals, but through modest assertions. Choosing to write by hand when you could type. Choosing to remember a friend's birthday without checking your phone's reminder. Choosing to be bored instead of instantly filling every empty moment with stimulation.

Boredom especially interests me. We've been taught that boredom is waste, that it represents time not spent productively or entertainingly. But boredom is actually when the mind does its most essential work. It's when the brain stops reacting to external stimulus and starts thinking for itself. Daydreaming, which is a form of boredom, is where ideas originate, where emotional processing happens, where you actually get to know yourself. The person who never allows themselves to be bored is someone who never develops their own interior landscape.

So maybe the rebellion is partly about boredom too—about allowing yourself to be unstimulated, unoptimized, genuinely unproductive in any measurable sense.

There's also something beautiful about the rebellion of attention. In a world competing frantically for your focus, choosing to give your full attention to one person, one book, one task, one moment becomes almost subversive. When someone puts their phone away during a conversation, they're announcing that you matter more than the infinite scroll. When someone reads the same book twice instead of moving to the next one, they're saying that depth matters more than coverage. These feel like small things, but they're not. They're statements about what you value and what you won't sell.

I think about skills that are becoming obsolete—the ability to navigate without GPS, to cook without recipes, to entertain yourself without entertainment technology, to sit with another person in silence without needing to fill it. These skills are becoming more valuable precisely as they become less necessary. They're becoming luxury goods in the sense that they represent freedom from dependence on systems.

And yet, I don't think the answer is wholesale rejection of modernity. That's a different kind of fantasy. We live in the modern world; we're shaped by it; we benefit from it in countless ways. The rebellion isn't about escaping into some imagined past, but about maintaining pockets of autonomy within the present.

What strikes me is how much energy these small rebellions require. It takes more effort to avoid optimization than to surrender to it. It's harder to live with intention than to drift with the current. But that difficulty is also what makes these choices meaningful. They're not inevitable; they're chosen. And choice, real choice about how you spend your consciousness and time, is increasingly the rarest commodity.

I think we're all searching for ways to be genuinely present in our own lives. To be the authors of our days rather than the subjects of someone else's system. To experience time as something to be inhabited rather than spent. To find meaning in the small, repeated acts that constitute a life rather than in the constant chasing of optimized outcomes.

The small rebellions are how we do this. They're how we say no to being merely efficient. They're how we insist on being human—which is to say inefficient, emotional, particular, and completely, stubbornly attached to the small rituals and choices that make us who we are.

So maybe make that coffee slowly. Read that book twice. Take the long way home. Remember something without searching for it. Be bored for an afternoon. Give someone your full attention. Choose the harder thing because it's yours.

These aren't revolutionary acts in the traditional sense. But perhaps that's what real revolution has always been: not the dramatic reshaping of everything, but the quiet, persistent assertion that your life belongs to you.
